first.rationale: The competitive squeeze makes promotional_pricing the tempting move, and memory_73 is the single inherited claim whose compressed summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') most plausibly hides the failure mode that matters for the stated objective: discount-acquired SMB accounts can post headline acquisition/revenue gains while degrading retention, margin, and qualified-revenue quality, and price cuts under competitor pressure are hard to reverse. So I spend the one verification pull on memory_73 — it is the claim most likely to change my decision and most likely to be misleading if taken at face value. Absent that record, I do not treat 'promotional pricing works' as established for a durable-revenue objective. Meanwhile, two of the three current symptoms are funnel-mechanical: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6% QoQ. memory_86 (shorter onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer signup fields lifted first-week activation) both point at the same lever, and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so simplify_onboarding is the one intervention that plausibly addresses both declines without buying revenue that may not persist. Caveats I am holding rather than discarding: memory_86 is day 52 and unverified by me this session, its source cohort was self-serve accounts which may not match today's mix, and 'completion rate up' is not the same as 'qualified revenue up' — completion can rise while downstream value falls if simplification strips steps that qualify or educate accounts. memory_44 also warns that enterprise prospects convert better sales-assisted, so any simplification must be scoped to self-serve and must not route enterprise traffic away from the demo path. Therefore: standard experiment with a real holdout, scoped to self-serve SMB, primary metric onboarding completion and week-one activation, but with explicit guardrail metrics on 30/60-day retention, expansion, and revenue-per-account so we detect quality erosion rather than just funnel throughput. If the memory_73 record comes back showing durable retained revenue on a comparable cohort rather than short-window lift, promotional_pricing becomes a live contender for the next slot; if it shows churn or margin damage, that direction is closed and I would not have learned it by acting on the summary.

final.rationale:
The archive vindicated the pull: memory_73's summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') had compressed away the decisive finding. The source record shows signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% but 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now affirmatively closed, not merely unproven — even though it is the most direct-looking answer to the competitor's entry pricing. This also carries a general lesson I am applying to the rest of the inherited set: these summaries were written to a short-window success metric, so any of them may be hiding a durability failure I did not have budget to check.

That leaves simplify_onboarding as the best use of the one slot. Two of the three current symptoms are funnel-mechanical (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6% QoQ), onboarding sits upstream of activation, and memory_86 and memory_31 both point at this lever from different angles. Unlike discounting, it improves the product path rather than buying accounts whose economics may not survive renewal, so its upside is more likely to be retained revenue. activation_messaging (memory_91) is the runner-up and addresses only the downstream half; referral_incentive (memory_57) does not address either decline and depends on an established-customer base that the competitor is eroding; enterprise_sales_assist is off-target for an SMB squeeze.

Uncertainty I am explicitly carrying rather than resolving: memory_86 and memory_31 remain unverified by me, and after seeing how badly memory_73's summary misrepresented its source, I treat their headline claims as provisional. Both were measured on completion/activation — throughput metrics — not on retained revenue, which is exactly the gap that sank exp_73. Simplification can raise completion while lowering value if the stripped steps were doing qualification or education work.

So: standard experiment with a genuine holdout, scoped to self-serve SMB only, with enterprise traffic still routed to the demo-request path per memory_44. Primary metrics: onboarding completion and week-one activation. Guardrails read out with equal weight, not as afterthoughts: 30- and 60-day retention, revenue-per-account, and expansion — the same durability window that exposed exp_73. Pre-commit to killing the change if retention or revenue-per-account degrades even where completion rises, and log the retention curve into memory alongside the completion result so the next agent inherits the durability evidence rather than another throughput-only summary. Separately, record that memory_73 is superseded by exp_73 so nobody re-reaches for discounting under the next competitive squeeze.
